new_statements.quote: Kru has both lexical and grammatical tone. Languages have either three or four register tones, which in this study will usually be marked in the following way: in a four-tone system, high tone will be marked by [˝], mid-high tone by [´], mid tone by [¯], and low tone by [`]. In three-tone systems, the symbol [´] will mark high, [¯] mid, and [`] low. In both three-tone and four-tone languages, mid tone is often unmarked. ... Tone plays an extremely important role in the grammatical systems of the Kru family, making such distinctions as perfective/imperfective aspect, possessive/relative/subject pronouns, definite/indefinite, and sometimes singular/plural.

new_statements.relation_note: Family-level: all Kru languages of the study (Cedepo among the data-source languages) have lexical and grammatical tone with three or four register tones; Cedepo forms are cited with tone marks (p. 42); nothing on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kru languages, including the Cedepo (Chedepo Grebo) data used in the study, are register-tone languages with three or four level tones carrying lexical and grammatical contrasts; the number of tones for Cedepo is not specified; no word stress is described.
new_statements.exceptions: contour tones analysed as sequences of register tones except a low falling tone in Wobé
new_statements.identity_note: Cedepo = Chedepo, the E Je/Chedepo dialect listed by Glottolog under Northern Grebo (nort2810); the cluster lists on p. 9 (after Ingemann & Duitsman) reproduce exactly the Northern Grebo dialect set (Palipo, Gbepo, Chedepo, Jedepo, Tienpo, Klepo; Nitiabo, Sabo, Tuobo, Ketiepo, Webo; Fopo-Bua). The tone statement itself is family-level ('Kru.. Languages have either three or four register tones') and does not say which count applies to Cedepo: group-level statement. [name in source: Cedepo (Grebo complex); Liberian Grebo cluster 7 'Palipo, Gbepo, Cedepo, Jedebo, Tiempo, Klepo', cluster 5 'Nitiabo, Sabo, Tuobo, Kitiapo, Webo', cluster 6 'Fopo and Bua'; pages 7-9 (classification, Map 3), 10 (summary list), 11 (data base: 'Cedepo - Jim Laesch'), 16 (1.4.1 Phonology: tone), 42 (Cedepo imperfective forms, tone-marked)]

new_statements.quote: Tone, as most of us already know, is an important part of the alphabets of Liberia's indigenous languages. ... The most common way of writing tone in Liberia is by the use of diacritics over the vowel; ' indicates that the pitch of the voice is relatively high, ` indicate that the pitch is relatively low, - indicates that the voice level is between the higher and lower levels of pitch, ^ indicates that the pitch level falls from high to low pitch level and [mark lost in scanned] represents low to high. Other variations involving mid tone in combination with other tones are common. The Chedepo alphabet marks high tone with a vertical mark or an apostrophe to eliminate the confusion that new readers of other languages have when distinguishing ' from `.
new_statements.citation: Duitsman, John (The Institute for Liberian Languages). 1976-77. Considerations in spelling Liberian names. Liberian Studies Journal VII(2): 133-143.

new_statements.relation_note: Tone is marked in the Chedepo alphabet (high tone = vertical mark or apostrophe); nothing on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chedepo (E Je, Northern Grebo) is written with lexical tone marks: high tone is marked with a vertical stroke or apostrophe in the Chedepo alphabet. Orthographic remark only; no tone inventory or analysis, nothing on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: General article on writing Liberian personal/place names; the tone section contains one first-hand remark on the 'Chedepo alphabet' -- Chedepo (= Chlehpo, the E Je reference dialect of the LBT/TILL Grebo programme) is a Northern Grebo dialect (nort2810). The rest of the article is not about this languoid.
